newsitem.title: USA: Storm sparks rise in oil prices, but cotton falls.
newsitem.headline: Storm sparks rise in oil prices, but cotton falls.

text.p: Crude oil prices rose Tuesday after winds from tropical storm Josephine forced oil wells and ports in the U.S. Gulf to shut down, but cotton fell on news that much of the southern crop survived the storm.
Hog and pork prices were buoyed by forecasts that hog shipments will decline when Midwest farmers concentrate on harvesting corn and soybeans.
Crude oil rallied on news the storm cut output in some fields and closed ports in the Gulf of Mexico.
"The port situation had to have lent support since it will tighten supplies," said a Texas oil trader.

Traders estimated the weekend storm cut Gulf crude production by 600,000 barrels. It also disrupted shipping at the deepwater Louisiana Offshore Oil Port and closed two major Mexican terminals. Restoring production will take time.
"It's not a matter of flipping switches and turning knobs," said one oil trader, who noted that workers needed to be transported back to the rigs.
Traders said the storm cut output in fields operated by British Petroleum, Mobil Corp. and Chevron Corp.

Crude oil for November delivery ended 30 cents higher at $25.54 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange. November heating oil fell 0.30 cent a gallon to 76.19 cents, but November gasoline was 0.16 cent higher at 66.50 per gallon.
Cotton at the New York Cotton Exchange moved lower after Josephine spared crops throughout the Southeast, industry sources said.
"This was a classic case of 'buy the rumour, sell the fact,'" said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes.
By late Tuesday, the storm was in New England and clear of U.S. cotton areas.

Cotton was also pressured by selling ahead of Friday's Agriculture Department crop report. Analysts said the government's crop estimate may be near 18.4 million 480-pound bales vs. 17.9 million in September.
"People didn't want to stay long the market going into the crop report," said Ganes.
Cotton for December delivery closed down 1.80 cents at 75.85 cents per pound.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, hog and pork belly futures closed sharly higher on supply worries.

Analysts said meat packers will likely raise bids for hogs Wednesday because there should be fewer hogs available. Clear weather will have farmers driving combines through corn and soybean fields rather than driving hogs to market.
Chuck Levitt, livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp., said hog slaughter will be down this week, which should also lift pork prices.
The expected drop in hog slaughter and pork production lifted pork belly futures as well. Pork bellies are the raw materials from which bacon is made.
Belly prices also attracted buying from traders reacting to rumours a storage report would show a drop in supplies.

After the close, the CME reported frozen belly supplies in reporting warehouses dropped 2.423 million pounds this past week, which exceeded trade estimates for a drop of 500,000 to 1.5 million pounds.
Hog futures for October delivery set a contract high of 60.300 cents per pound and settled at 59.925 cents, up 0.900 cent. February pork bellies settled 2.725 cents higher at 78.875 cents per pound.
